sec.title: Background
sec.p: Bipolar Disorder (BD) is a class of mood disorders that poses a significant diagnostic challenge for clinicians. With its unknown etiology and the increasing disability burden it contributes to, BD necessitates further study to improve patient outcomes. Our study aimed to characterize the demographic trends in BD-related mortality using the CDC WONDER database.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: The CDC WONDER database was utilized to collect data on the mortality burden from 1999 to 2023. Data was stratified by race or ethnicity, sex, age, rural or urban designation, and census region. Data analysis was performed using Joinpoint analysis to help determine trends as well as statistical significance.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Our study found that the rate at which BD was mentioned in death certificates increased throughout the study period and mortality associated with BD increased with age. Additionally, the study found statistically significant increases in age adjusted mortality rate when analyzed in groups. Not only was mortality rate determined to be higher amongst females than their male counterparts, variation by race and ethnicity also persisted, with mortality being highest among the Non-Hispanic White cohort. Mortality burden varied by region, with higher mortality rates in rural areas than in urban areas and in the Midwest United States, compared to other census regions.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Our study expands on prior research related to trends in mortality of BD and aims to highlight the disproportionate mortality burdens related to BD as a potential guide towards future management strategies. Further studies related to how the increased utilization of mental health resources, including telehealth, and focus on earlier treatment initiation can be useful to guide mental health practices in the future.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Bipolar Disorder (BD), also known as Bipolar Affective Disorder, is a class of psychiatric conditions characterized by alternating periods of mania and depression (Vincenzo et al. 2024). A collection of disorders, BD includes diagnoses such as Bipolar I disorder, which requires the presence of at least one manic episode, and Bipolar II disorder, which necessitates the presence of at least one hypomanic and one major depressive episode, among other similar diagnoses (Vincenzo et al. 2024). BD is a clinical challenge, often going undiagnosed or misdiagnosed (Goes 2023). Though the etiology of the disorder is largely unknown, understanding the risk factors and presentation of the disorder is vital to early identification and treatment (Rowland and Marwaha 2018). With a lifetime prevalence of 1% for Bipolar I in the United States (US) and a mean age of onset in the early twenties, better understanding the impact of the disorder is of growing importance (Rowland and Marwaha 2018).

In addition to posing a diagnostic challenge, BD is a leading cause of global disability and a major cause of early mortality, stemming from suicides, homicides, accidents, and medical comorbidities (Vincenzo et al. 2024; Hayes et al. 2015). Many studies outline the association between BD and risk of suicide, with premature mortality from suicide being 11 times higher in individuals with BD than without (Hayes et al. 2015; Biazus et al. 2023; Pike et al. 2024). Now, there is growing evidence that mortality risk from natural causes is also increased in BD, including from metabolic, cardiovascular, and infectious disease (Biazus et al. 2023). This is attributable not only to increased incidence, but also to delayed diagnosis and treatment, decreased access to quality medical care and screening, and common medication side effects (Biazus et al. 2023; Solmi et al. 2021; Vancampfort et al. 2016; Goldstein et al. 2020). Medication management for BD includes mood stabilizers, including lithium, divalproex, and antipsychotics, including aripiprazole, quetiapine, and risperidone (Vincenzo et al. 2024). Second generation antipsychotics, particularly olanzapine and quetiapine, are associated with an increased risk of metabolic and cardiovascular side effects (Holt 2019). These include effects such as diabetes, weight gain, and QT prolongation. Moreover, patients treated with the antipsychotics olanzapine and risperidone had higher all-cause mortality from either natural or unnatural causes than those treated with lithium (Chan et al. 2024). Interestingly, prior research on the effects of lithium on chronic corticosteroid use in rats found that lithium treatment reduced insulin resistance (Delangre et al. 2013). This opens a novel avenue for research into the relationship between lithium use and insulin resistance in humans. Ultimately, it is vital to recognize the tremendous risk BD can pose to patients, not just through symptoms of the disorder, but also through the ways in which it is managed.

As such, this study aims to characterize the demographic trends in BD-associated mortality using the CDC WONDER database to elucidate disparities in care for patients with the disorder. The goal is to guide future management strategies and to mitigate the disproportionate mortality burdens of the disorder detailed in this report.

sec.title: Data collection
sec.p: The Center for Disease Control and Prevention Wide-ranging Online Data for Epidemiologic Research (CDC WONDER) database was utilized to collect data on the BD-related mortality burden in the US between 1999 and 2023 (CDC WONDER 2025a). CDC WONDER utilizes the 10th revision of the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-10) codes to categorize different causes of mortality in patients based on their death certificates (Minhas et al. 2025). This data, which is deidentified and publicly available through this online database, was probed to identify cases in which BD was listed as one of the contributory causes of patient mortality using ICD-10 code F31, which correlates to BD. Our analysis focuses in on this narrow subset of the population, and it is important to note that our data may exclude the full clinical range of bipolar-spectrum patients encoded under F30, which encodes patients who have had a manic episode.

Through this study’s analysis, data was stratified by sex, race or ethnicity, age, rural or urban designation, and census region. Sex categories included were male and female and race and ethnicity was grouped into non-Hispanic (NH) White, NH Black, Asian and Pacific Islander, and Hispanic or Latino (National Institutes of Health 2025a). Seven different 10-year age cohorts were analyzed, including 25–34 years, 35–44 years, 45–54 years, 55–64 years, 65–74 years, 75–84 years, and over 84 years. Urban and rural designation was made based on the National Center for Health Statistics stratification of US counties into one of six metropolitan or nonmetropolitan cohorts based on population size and level of urbanization (CDC National Center for Health Statistics 2024a). Patients’ legal state of residence at the time of death was utilized to group data into four different census regions, including the Northeast, Midwest, South, and West (CDC WONDER 2025b).

sec.title: Data analysis
sec.p: Age-adjusted mortality rate (AAMR) was calculated by applying age-specific rates to a standardized age distribution, the 2000 US standard population, determined by CDC WONDER for each of the different demographic variables outlined above. Joinpoint analysis is a statistical software used to model trends in data, helping to determine their statistical significance (CDC National Center for Health Statistics 2024b; National Cancer Institute n.d.). This modeling strategy is helpful to identify specific years in which significant changes to the data trends occurred, and these specific points are called joinpoints. Each interval between these joinpoints can be mapped with individual regression lines (Ebrahimi et al. 2025). Using Joinpoint analysis, annual percentage change (APC) and average annual percentage change (AAPC) and their 95% confidence intervals (CI) were determined. APC is used to describe the rate at which AAMR changed by year over our study period. AAPC reflects the average rate of change in AAMR over the course of the study. This data was analyzed and has been compiled and included below.

sec.title: Overall
sec.p: From 1999 to 2023, there were 67,098 deaths related to BD in the US (Table 1). Overall, the AAMR increased from 0.4 (95% CI 0.37 to 0.43) in 1999 to 1.73 in 2023, with a peak AAMR of 1.84 in 2022. The average annual percentage change (AAPC) during the study period was 6.19* (95% CI 5.50 to 7.63). The annual percentage change (APC) in AAMR was 24.87* (95% CI 12.59 to 46.75) between 1999 and 2002, which decreased to 3.76* (95% CI 3.19 to 4.30) from 2002 to 2023. Overall, AAMR was lowest in 1999, and generally continued to increase throughout the time of the study.

sec.title: Sex
sec.p: From 1999 to 2023, BD was listed as a cause in 38,471 deaths among females and 28,627 deaths in males. The AAMR increased in females from 0.42 in 1999 to 1.78 (95% CI 1.71 to 1.85) in 2023, with a peak AAMR of 1.90 (95% CI 1.83 to 1.98) in 2020. The AAPC in females from 1999 to 2023 was 6.34* (95% CI 5.28 to 7.82). The APC in AAMR was 38.67* (95% CI 11.50 to 63.47) between 1999 and 2001, which decreased to 3.81* (95% CI 3.23 to 4.33) from 2001 to 2023. In females, the overall AAMR was lowest in 1999 and continued to gradually increase throughout the time of the study.

In males, the AAMR increased from 0.38 (95% CI in 0.33 to 0.42) in 1999 to 1.64 (95% CI 1.57 to 1.72) in 2023, with a peak AAMR of 1.78 (95% CI 1.71 to 1.86) in 2022. The AAPC in males from 1999 to 2023 was 6.20 (95% CI 5.49 to 7.55). The APC in AAMR was 26.31* (95% CI 16.44 to 45.78) from 1999 to 2002, which decreased to 3.17* (95% CI 0.95 to 4.97) from 2002 to 2018. The APC in AAMR rose again to 10.06 (95% CI -0.82 to 12.75) from 2018 to 2021, prior to decreasing to -2.12 (95% CI -8.78 to 6.69) between 2021 and 2023. In males, the overall AAMR was lowest in 1999 and generally continued to increase throughout the time of the study (Table 1; Fig. 1).

This figure reflects how mortality rate changed overall and among males and females over the study period. Overall, the mortality rate increased over the study period, with the lowest mortality rate in 1999. Similar trends were observed among males and females, with mortality increasing, overall, across the study period. sec.title: Race and ethnicity
sec.p: Non-Hispanic White people had the highest AAMR throughout the study period, increasing from 0.47 (95% CI 0.44 to 0.51) in 1999 to 2.03 (95% CI 1.96 to 2.10) in 2023, with a peak AAMR of 2.21 (95% CI 2.14 to 2.29) in 2022 (Table 2). The AAPC during this time period was 5.78* (95% CI 4.97 to 7.23). The APC was 16.42* (95% CI 7.79 to 35.21) between 1999 and 2003, which reduced to 3.77* (95% CI 3.09 to 4.36) from 2003 to 2023.

sec.p: The NH Black population had the second greatest increase in AAMR throughout the study period, starting at an AAMR of 0.19 (95% CI 0.13 to 0.28) in 1999 to 1.50 (95% CI 1.35 to 1.64) in 2023, with a peak AAMR of 1.6 (95% CI 1.45 to 1.75) in 2020 (Table 2). The AAPC during this time period was 8.87* (95% CI 7.96 to 10.45). The APC was 31.28* (95% CI 15.94 to 67.72) from 1999 to 2002, which fell to 5.01* (95% CI 3.45 to 5.90) between the years 2002 and 2017. Subsequently, the APC increased to 18.59* (95% CI 12.14 to 22.30) from 2017 to 2020, before decreasing to -0.75 (95% CI -6.42 to 2.76) from 2020 to 2023.

Mortality data for the Hispanic and Latino population was reported from 2000 onwards, due to lack of significant sample size and unreliable data from 1999. The Hispanic and Latino population experienced the smallest increase in AAMR throughout the study, starting at 0.22 (95% CI 0.13 to 0.34) in 2000 and increasing to 0.86 (95% CI 0.75 to 0.96) in 2023, with a peak AAMR of 0.88 (95% CI 0.77 to 0.99) in 2020. The AAPC from 2000 to 2023 was 6.54* (95% CI 5.68 to 7.88) (Table 2; Fig. 2).

As reflected in the data, mortality rate was consistently highest among the NH White population, followed by the NH Black and Hispanic and Latino populations, respectively. Generally, mortality remained lowest in the Asian and Pacific Islander cohort. Across all race and ethnicity categories analyzed, mortality rate increased in 2023 compared to 1999 (left). Among the Hispanic and Latino population, mortality increased consistently at an APC of 6.54* from 2000 to 2023. *Indicates statistically significant APC values

sec.title: Age
sec.p: Throughout the study period, BD-related mortality increased with older age. Individuals over the age of 85 had the highest crude mortality rate (CMR) among all of the ten-year age cohorts, with a crude mortality rate of 2.82 (95% CI 2.31 to 3.33) in 1999, increasing to 6.39 (95% CI 5.76 to 7.02) in 2023. Peak crude mortality rate for this age group was 7.15 (95% CI 6.47 to 7.82) in 2021. During this time, the AAPC was 3.49* (95% CI 2.13 to 5.36). Joinpoint analysis reflected that the APC decreased from 13.50* (95% CI 3.18 to 46.71) between 1999 and 2003 to 1.59 (95% CI -0.38 to 2.35) between 2003 and 2023.

For individuals between the ages of 75 to 84, the CMR went from 1.73 (95% CI 1.49 to 1.96) in 1999 to 5.05 (95% CI 4.72 to 5.37) in 2023, reaching its highest value of 5.17 (95% CI 4.83 to 5.51) in 2022. The AAPC for this cohort during the study period was 4.09* (95% CI 3.56 to 4.66). Moreover, the APC from 1999 to 2002 was 20.03* (95% CI 12.66 to 32.54), 0.62 (-0.16 to 1.19) from 2002 to 2016, and 9.59* (95% CI 6.71 to 13.69) from 2016 to 2020. Crude mortality then fell significantly, with an APC of -1.28 (-6.17 to 1.69) from 2020 to 2023.

Next, individuals aged 65 to 74 had a CMR of 0.93 (95% CI 0.79 to 1.07) in 1999, which increased to 3.73 (95% CI 3.53 to 3.93) in 2023. The AAPC from 1999 to 2023 was calculated to be 5.83* (95% CI 4.89 to 7.08). From 1999 to 2001, APC was 24.52* (95% CI 5.48 to 44.36). This value decreased to 3.27 (95% CI -1.21 to 3.94) between 2001 and 2017 and increased again to 13.61* (95% CI 7.36 to 17.10) between 2017 and 2020. APC between 2020 and 2023 in this age group was 0.79 (95% CI -5.77 to 4.46).

The BD-related CMR for individuals aged 55 to 64 was 0.41 (95% CI 0.30 to 0.50) in 1999 and 2.53 (95% CI 2.37 to 2.68) in 2023. AAPC during the study period was 7.79* (95% CI 6.80 to 9.35). From 1999 to 2001, APC was 33.26* (95% CI 12.23 to 56.84). This value decreased to 6.32* (95% CI 5.76 to 7.27) between 2001 and 2021, before decreasing further to 0.006 (95% CI -5.27 to 5.90) between 2021 and 2023.

Amongst individuals aged 45 to 54, BD-related CMR was 0.22 (95% CI 0.17 to 0.27) in 1999, increasing to 1.16 (95% CI 1.05 1.26) in 2023. AAPC was reported as 6.89* (95% CI 6.22 to 7.86). The APC between 1999 and 2007 was 15.73* (95% CI 12.40 to 20.73) and 2.73* (95% CI 1.88 to 3.50) between 2007 and 2023.

The CMR in individuals aged 34 to 45 was 0.1 (95% CI 0.07 to 0.13) in 1999 and 0.68 (95% CI 0.60 to 0.75) in 2023. The AAPC for this group was 8.62* (95% CI 7.86 to 9.86) during this time. APC went from 52.34* (95% CI 31.99 to 74.50) between 1999 and 2001 to 12.91* (95% CI 8.50 to 17.00) between 2001 and 2007, 0.29 (95% CI -5.84 to 1.66) between 2007 and 2016, and finally increased to 5.70* (95% CI 3.73 to 12.12) from 2016 to 2023 (Fig. 3).

sec.p: The youngest cohort studied, aged 25 to 34, had the lowest CMR related to BD. Mortality data for this cohort was reported beginning 2000, due to small sample size and lack of statistically significant data in 1999. This cohort had a CMR of 0.1 (95% CI 0.07 to 0.14) in 2000, which increased to 0.38 (95% CI 0.33 to 0.44) in 2023. In this cohort, the AAPC was 6.03* (95% CI 4.19 to 9.21), and APC decreased from 13.29* (95% CI 5.47 to 56.53) between 2000 and 2006 to 3.57 (95% CI -0.14 to 4.68) between 2006 and 2023. CMR by age can be found in Table 3.

sec.title: Rural v. urban
sec.p: When comparing populated regions, BD-related AAMR was initially similar between the rural and urban populations. However, the AAMR in rural areas was higher by the end of the study period when compared to urban areas. Rural areas saw an AAMR of 0.47 (95% CI 0.39 to 0.55) in 1999 increase to 2.36 (95% CI 2.20 to 2.52) in 2020, with an AAPC of 7.38* (95% CI 6.26 to 9.32). Urban areas saw the AAMR increase from 0.40 (95% CI 0.36 to 0.43) in 1999 to 1.70 (95% CI 1.65 to 1.76) in 2020, with AAPC of 6.35* (95% CI 5.65 to 7.29). The APC of the urban areas had multiple significant changes throughout the years. The APC was 24.45* (95% CI 11.90 to 37.67) from 1999 to 2001, before decreasing to 6.42* (95% CI 3.73 to 8.61) between 2001 and 2007. The urban APC then decreased between 2007 and 2016 to 2.14 (95% CI -1.31 to 2.90), before increasing again to 7.56* (95% CI 5.08 to 13.41) between 2016 and 2020. The APC of the rural areas only had one significant change. The rural APC was 27.38* (95% CI 13.09 to 59.73) from 1999 to 2002, before decreasing to 4.36* (95% CI 3.57 to 5.10) from 2002 to 2020 (Table 4; Fig. 4).

sec.title: Census
sec.p: Throughout the study period, each census region saw an increase in AAMR. The Midwest saw the greatest increase in BD-related AAMR between 1999 and 2023, increasing from 0.44 (95% CI 0.37 to 0.50) in 1999 to 1.87 (95% CI 1.75 to 1.98) in 2023. The peak AAMR for the Midwest was 2.08 (95% CI 1.96 to 2.21) in 2020. The APC of the Midwest was 27.93* (95% CI 15.94 to 49.62) from 1999 to 2002 before decreasing to 3.24* (95% CI 2.81 to 3.67) from 2002 to 2023. Overall, the AAPC of the Midwest was 6.05* (95% CI 5.19 to 6.02).

The census region with the next greatest increase in BD-related AAMR was the West, with an increase in AAMR from 0.51 (95% CI 0.44 to 0.59) in 1999 to 1.96 (95% CI 1.85 to 2.07) in 2023. The peak AAMR for the West was 2.05 (95% CI 1.93 to 2.16). The APC of the West was 18.68* (95% CI 11.22 to 34.09) from 1999 to 2003 before decreasing to 3.33* (95% CI 2.89 to 3.78) from 2003 to 2023. The AAPC of the West was 5.74* (95% CI 5.10 to 6.81).

The AAMR for the South was 0.35 (95% CI 0.30 to 0.40) in 1999, which increased to 1.96 (95% CI 1.85 to 2.07) in 2023, with a peak of 2.05 (95% CI 1.93 to 2.16) in 2022. The APC of the South had multiple significant changes throughout the time period of the study. The APC began at 26.74* (95% CI 13.37 to 40.87) from 1999 to 2001 before decreasing to 7.43* (95% CI 4.30 to 9.67) from 2001 to 2008. The APC decreased once more to 1.68 (95% CI -3.91 to 3.12) from 2008 to 2016 before increasing to 9.05* (95% CI 7.08 to 13.94) from 2016 to 2021. Finally, the APC decreased to -1.13 (95% CI -5.64 to 3.72) from 2021 to 2023. The South experienced the highest AAPC of 6.53* (95% CI 5.94 to 7.43) (Table 5).

sec.p: The AAMR for the Northeast was 0.40 (95% CI 0.34 to 0.47) in 1999, which increased to 1.42 (95% CI 1.31 to 1.53) in 2023, with a peak AAMR of 1.70 (95% CI 1.58 to 1.82) in 2020. The AAPC of the Northeast was the lowest at 4.51* (95% CI 3.82 to 5.37), and there was not a significant change in the APC throughout the study period (Table 5; Fig. 5).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This study sought to utilize the CDC WONDER database in order to characterize the demographic trends in BD-related mortality. A key finding of our study was that the AAMR related to BD was found to be continuously higher in females when compared to males. When looking at how sex may affect bipolar symptoms and comorbidities, studies have shown that the onset of bipolar disorder tends to occur later in women than men (Arnold 2003). Additionally, women more often have a seasonal pattern of mood disturbance. Women also experience major depressive episodes, mixed mania, and rapid cycling more often than men (Arnold 2003). Comorbidities can differ between men and women, with men more likely to have substance use disorder while women are more likely to have comorbid anxiety, thyroid disease, and migraines (Piccirilli et al. 2025). This increased risk of psychiatric and medical comorbidities may explain the higher AAMR noted among women. Additionally, the increased risk of rapid cycling may increase their risk of hospitalization and suicidal behaviors (Piccirilli et al. 2025). Previous studies have also examined how there may be gender differences in suicide for patients with BD. One study found that although there is no significant difference in suicide ideation between gender, males have a higher prevalence of suicide deaths while women have a higher prevalence of suicide attempts (Hu et al. 2023). Interestingly, prior studies have highlighted how the ratio of male to female suicides is narrower in BD than that of the general population (Amini et al. 2025). Others have also highlighted how the increased likelihood of major depressive episodes among women may cause an increased risk of misdiagnosis of unipolar depression as opposed to bipolar disorder (Rastelli et al. 2013). This can lead to delayed proper treatment and potential triggering of a manic or hypomanic episode. Future studies should investigate specific reasons as to why BD may be a more common cause of death among females despite overall higher suicide risk among male patients.

AAMR related to BD was highest in the NH White population. Studies show that this cohort is more likely to be diagnosed with BD, whereas individuals of other racial groups are more likely to be misdiagnosed and therefore not be coded for as accurately using F31 (Tchikrizov et al. 2023). This can explain why BD-associated complications, including mortality in patients with this diagnosis reported in our study, is higher in the NH White group. The second highest AAMR associated with BD was reported in NH Black patients. Despite presenting with findings of BD, NH Black patients often experience inadequate treatment, commonly due to their symptoms being attributed to a different diagnosis (Akinhanmi et al. 2018). A recent study found that NH Black patients were less likely than their NH White counterparts to be prescribed lithium, lamotrigine, and carbamazepine, key mood stabilizers used in the treatment of BD (Tchikrizov et al. 2023). Therefore, despite an ultimate classification of their presentation as BD, the increased mortality in this group may be explained by an exacerbation of symptoms and mania due to inadequate initial care. Hispanic and Latino patients presented with the third highest mortality rate related to BD, but they have been found to be less likely to pursue psychiatric care and take their prescribed medications than NH White patients overall (Salcedo et al. 2017). Finally, Asian and Pacific Islander patients were found to have the lowest overall BD-related mortality, which may be influenced by the culture’s historical avoidance of and stigma surrounding mental health diagnoses (Woo 2017). Future studies should examine discrepancies in diagnoses and treatment of BD among various racial groups to ensure quality of care and more accurate overall mortality assessments.

Throughout the study period, mortality associated with BD increased. Patients with BD remain at increased risk of premature mortality than the general population, attributable to causes including suicide, homicide, substance abuse, and comorbid medical illnesses (Yocum et al. 2023). Studies report that more people are being diagnosed with BD in recent years than before. With revisions to criteria to expand the collection of symptoms and duration qualifiers for diagnosis, more individuals are being diagnosed with BD and associated disorders to avoid missing early detection and inappropriately treating them for major depressive disorder (Glick 2004). Moreover, the utilization of mental health resources has generally continued to increase throughout our study period, which could coincide with decreased stigma surrounding mental health conditions (Wang et al. 2023). Despite this overall decrease in stigma, however, certain mental health conditions still face harsh perceptions, such as increasing public perceptions of likely violence among patients with schizophrenia (Pescosolido et al. 2021). Thus, further studies aimed at how the stigma related to BD has shifted throughout the years and its effect on utilization of mental health resources could be beneficial.

Across all age groups studied, the mortality rate related to BD increased over time. The 85 + age cohort had the highest CMR, while the 25–34 year age cohort had the lowest average CMR. A prior study looking at standardized mortality rate (SMR), which demonstrates the relative mortality rate associated with BD compared to that of the overall population, for patients aged 15–64 with BD between 1965 and 2014 found that SMR was highest in the 15–29 age group and lowest in the 60–64 year age group (Staudt Hansen et al. 2019). The study notes that compared to the overall population, there is higher mortality associated with BD in younger cohorts that their older counterparts (Staudt Hansen et al. 2019). Though our study reports absolute mortality using CMR as a metric, temporal variations in utilization of mental health services in more recent years may explain the trends identified by Staudt Hansen et al. (Wang et al. 2023) In addition, there has been a shift towards early detection and intervention in psychiatry that has allowed patients to begin treatment for BD earlier (Howes and Falkenberg 2011). This is important as longer durations of untreated illness is associated with greater morbidity and decreased response to mood stabilizer treatment (Howes and Falkenberg 2011). The ability to prevent the disorder from becoming increasingly severe early on and increasing overall life span into old age, when other comorbidities may become more prevalent, could offer a possible explanation for the CMR trends noted in our study. Older age bipolar disorder (OABD) is defined as bipolar disorder over the age of 50. Special consideration should be given to treating patients with OABD. This is due to the variability in clinical course that can be present in OABD patients. For example, some patients may have treatment resistance, shorter time between mood episodes, physical comorbidities, and decreased cognitive functioning (Beunders et al. 2023). Prior studies have highlighted how these comorbidities, such as cardiovascular disease and diabetes mellitus, were associated with an increased risk of mortality in patients with bipolar disorder in comparison to the general population (Crump et al. 2013). Studies examining cognitive dysfunction have noted that the cognitive impairment persists in both the mood attack and the remission stages, leading to impaired functional outcomes (Huang et al. 2023). As cognitive dysfunction and physical comorbidities remain prevalent in patients with OABD, further investigation as to how to best treat this disease is important (Beunders et al. 2023; Crump et al. 2013).

AAMR associated with BD was also notably higher in rural than urban US. Rural communities face significant barriers to accessing healthcare resources, including mental health services. Studies have shown that patients residing in rural areas generally had decreased utilization of mental health services, increased emergency department admissions, and increased suicide rates (Edwards et al. 2023). Barriers to accessing psychiatric services, including high cost and lack of mental health resources, in rural underserved communities lead more patients to pursue care in emergency departments (Onoye et al. 2013). A study of rural and urban patients with private insurance noted that patients in rural areas were less likely to pursue outpatient visits for mental health care and were more likely to rely on primary care providers than specialists when they did seek care (Chen et al. 2022). Moreover, stigma around mental health is reportedly higher in rural areas (Forrest et al. 2023; Prazak et al. 2024). This stigma, coupled with decreased access to care, may cause many patients to delay pursuing care for BD, leading to exacerbation of symptoms and escalation of suicidal thoughts and rates.

Finally, regional BD-related mortality findings correlated with the results found when data was stratified by rural vs. urban assignments. AAMR associated with BD was highest in the Midwest. Compared to other parts of the US, the Midwest has a greater proportion of people living in rural areas [44]. As such, increasing mortality associated with BD may be explained by the stigma and lack of access to resources experienced by individuals living in this region. Despite the lower population density of these rural areas, the lack of providers, geographic barriers to care, greater access to firearms, and stigma around help-seeking behaviors can complicate BD and lead to poorer outcomes, including suicidal thoughts (Stone and Crosby 2014; Andrilla et al. 2018). The West had the second highest mortality related to BD, after the Midwest. Here, the higher population density of the West could offer an explanation for increased BD-associated mortality. Nine of ten states in the US with the highest rates of suicide were located in the West (Stone and Crosby 2014). Despite the social determinants of health influencing mortality associated with BD in the Midwest, higher population sizes in the West could reflect increased rates of suicide, including from mental health conditions like BD. Furthermore, the Northeast US had the lowest BD-related mortality across all census regions studied, which may correlate to this region having the highest per capita supply of mental health providers, including psychiatrists, psychologists, and psychiatric nurse practitioners in the US (Andrilla et al. 2018).

sec.title: Future directions and limitations
sec.p: Our results highlight the need to address the disproportionate mortality burdens related to BD. This study builds upon findings from previous research and can be utilized to guide future public health strategies. Previous research has noted how stigma can play a role in delayed diagnosis and utilization of mental health resources; thus, public health initiatives aimed at continuing to destigmatize mental health are critical. Additionally, the expansion of telehealth can serve as a valuable resource to increase access to mental health services in areas that lack access to such resources. This study is not without limitations. Firstly, the data analyzed in this study is limited to the information and classification available in the CDC WONDER database. The CDC WONDER database, which uses death certificate information to classify cause of death, may leave room for interpretation by the provider filing the certificate (Iftikhar et al. 2025). The use of this study’s target ICD-10 code, F31, solely includes cases where mortality was associated with BD, as listed on these certificates. As such, it represents only this narrow definition of the collection of disorders that BD entails. This may lead to an underestimation of the true burden of BD-related mortality. Moreover, no information is provided on specific underlying or contributory causes of mortality in these patients beyond the association with BD, be it cardiovascular, cerebrovascular disease, suicide, or other. The data cannot be organized by treatment exposure, so we are not able to assess. Further study is required to elucidate the mechanisms of mortality in this cohort. Additionally, as our data examines BD as a whole, we are unable to differentiate mortality from Bipolar I, Bipolar II, and other subclassifications of the disorder (Aguglia et al. 2024). In addition, certain states, be it mania or depression, may predominate among different patients. This primary polarity is of vital importance to guiding individualized care and treatment. However, our data cannot separate mortality based on the primary symptoms of the patient’s presentation (Bartoli et al. 2024a, 2024b). At last, our query, due to data availability, is unable to assess BD-associated mortality by urbanization status beyond 2020.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: This study expands on prior research related to trends in mortality related to BD. Our study aims to highlight the disproportionate mortality burdens related to BD as a potential guide towards future management strategies. Researchers report multiple disparities in mortality rates, particularly in the older-age, rural, and NH white populations. Future studies exploring potential causes for these disparities, such as limited access to resources or stigma within communities, can be beneficial. Additionally, further studies examining the increased utilization of mental health resources, including telehealth, and a focus on earlier treatment initiation can be useful to guide mental health practices in the future.
